title: JESUS ACKNOWLEDGED PEOPLE WHOSE BODIES AND SEXUAL FUTURES DIDN’T FIT ORDINARY EXPECTATIONS
paragraphs:
JESUS ACKNOWLEDGED PEOPLE WHOSE BODIES AND SEXUAL FUTURES DIDN’T FIT ORDINARY EXPECTATIONS
We have sometimes made Christianity sound as though everyone must fit one respectable human pattern. Then Jesus spoke about people who didn’t—and He did it without pretending they weren’t there.
And then there are verses that read you.
It sits quietly inside a conversation about marriage, divorce, faithfulness, and the cost of discipleship. It is easy to move past because the language feels strange to modern ears.
But if you slow down, something startling happens.
Jesus acknowledges human lives that did not fit the ordinary expectation of marriage, sexual union, biological children, and family continuation.
And before anyone turns that word into a weapon for today's cultural battles, we need enough humility to let Jesus speak in His own historical and biblical context.
Because what He actually says is powerful enough.
The disciples have just heard Jesus give an uncompromising teaching about marriage. Their response is almost comically human:
“If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.”
And suddenly the conversation becomes much bigger than the disciples expected.
In the Greek text of Matthew 19:12, we read:

“εἰσὶν γὰρ εὐνοῦχοι οἵτινες ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς ἐγεννήθησαν οὕτως, καὶ εἰσὶν εὐνοῦχοι οἵτινες εὐνουχίσθησαν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ εἰσὶν εὐνοῦχοι οἵτινες εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.”

“For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”
He knew some people would never travel the expected road.
Literally, in context: they were born “thus” from their mother’s womb.
Others had this condition imposed upon them by human beings.
Others embraced celibacy for the kingdom of heaven.
And Jesus knew all three existed.
But we also need to say what the verse does not say.
Jesus was not using “eunuch” as a technical first-century synonym for “gay,” “transgender,” “intersex,” “asexual,” or any other modern identity category.
Those categories come from different historical and conceptual worlds, and forcing them directly into the Greek word εὐνοῦχος can make Scripture say more than Scripture actually says.
Biblical faithfulness does not require exaggeration.
Truth does not need our help.
The astonishing statement already sitting on the page is enough:
Jesus explicitly recognized people whose bodies, circumstances, or chosen devotion meant their sexual and reproductive futures did not follow the ordinary marital pattern expected by society.
And He did not speak as though such people were invisible.
Maybe that matters more than we realize.
Because religious communities can become very good at creating templates.
And for many people, marriage and family are extraordinary gifts from God.
Jesus Himself reaches back to creation in this very chapter:
He speaks of a man leaving father and mother and being joined to his wife, and He treats that covenant with tremendous seriousness.
So this passage is not Jesus dismantling marriage.
It is Jesus refusing to make marriage the definition of a complete human life.
Because standing in front of the disciples was the most complete human being who ever lived.
The Son of God never needed sexual experience to become fully human.
He never needed marriage to establish His worth.
He never needed biological children to leave an eternal legacy.
His identity was rooted in the Father.
His love was not smaller because it was not expressed through marriage.
His life was not incomplete because it did not follow the expected domestic script.
That should destroy one of the cruelest lies many people quietly carry:
“If my life doesn't look like everyone else's, something must be fundamentally wrong with me.”
Maybe you sit in church while another wedding is announced and everybody celebrates, while something inside you aches.
Maybe your body carries circumstances nobody around you understands.
Maybe your sexual desires have become an arena of painful conflict between what you feel and what you believe obedience to Christ requires.
Maybe you have questions you are terrified to say aloud because you already know how quickly Christians can reach for labels.
Maybe your story is so complicated that you stopped telling it.
You learned which questions were safe.
You learned how to say, “I'm doing fine.”
But God knows what happens after everybody goes home.
He knows the body you inhabit.
He knows what happened to you.
You do not have to lie to Jesus.
That is one of the most beautiful things about Him.
People may demand a polished testimony.
People may be frightened by complexity.
People may reduce you to one part of your story.
But there is another mistake we must avoid.
Compassion does not mean pretending Jesus never calls anyone to repentance.
The Gospel is not, “Come to Jesus and He will affirm everything you already believe about yourself.”
Then discover what it means to truly live.
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
That invitation does not single out one category of sinner.
It reaches the sexually immoral and the self-righteous.
The person consumed by lust and the person consumed by greed.
The person whose private browser history would humiliate them and the religious person secretly delighted to condemn them.
Nobody walks into the Kingdom carrying a certificate that says:
The scandal of Christianity is not that certain people are sinners.
The scandal is that all of us are.
And the greater scandal is what God did about it.
The Gospel does not begin with our ability to repair ourselves.
The innocent One bearing the judgment of the guilty.
Because sin is more serious than modern culture wants to admit.
And grace is more astonishing than religious people sometimes allow themselves to believe.
At Calvary, Jesus does not tell sinners to clean themselves up enough to become lovable.
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after the affair was confessed.
Not after the secret relationship ended.
Not after the identity questions were resolved.
Not after the religious hypocrisy was exposed.
But grace does not leave us where it found us.
The same Jesus who forgives says:
And following Jesus eventually puts every identity, every desire, every relationship, every ambition, every wound, every appetite, every dream, and every future at His feet.
Christianity is not ultimately about discovering the perfect label for yourself.
It is about belonging to Christ.
Paul says something breathtaking in Galatians 2:20:
That is Christian identity at its deepest level.
And perhaps that is why Matthew 19 becomes even more beautiful when we remember another eunuch later in the New Testament.
Acts 8 takes us onto a desert road.
A powerful man entrusted with the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.
A man whose embodied and social existence placed him outside the ordinary reproductive future is sitting in a chariot reading about a suffering Servant.
The eunuch asks the question that changes everything:
“About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this?”
“Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.”
And while traveling down the road, they encounter water.
That question almost hurts when you understand it.
My inability to fit the expected future?
And then Scripture says he “went on his way rejoicing.”
A person who might have been defined by what had happened to his body becomes defined by his relationship to Jesus Christ.
A person whose future did not look ordinary discovers that God's Kingdom is larger than ordinary human expectations.
And there is an even deeper biblical echo behind his story.
Isaiah had spoken directly to eunuchs centuries earlier.
Isaiah 56 records God's promise to those who keep His covenant:
“I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters.”
A name better than sons and daughters.
For someone unable to produce the descendants ancient societies considered essential to legacy, those words must have sounded almost impossible.
Your story does not end where human expectation ends.
You can have a name in My house.
Your life can carry eternal significance even when it cannot produce the future society expected from you.
And then, generations later, an Ethiopian eunuch sits on a road reading Isaiah.
Tell me Scripture is not beautiful.
The Bible's answer to human difference is not that every difference automatically becomes holy.
Neither is its answer that everyone who differs from the social norm should be treated as spiritually disposable.
Jesus gives people a name no human circumstance can finally erase.
Jesus does not save us because our desires are perfect.
He saves us because His mercy is.
And He does not merely forgive us so we can return unchanged to whatever enslaved us.
Sometimes through battles nobody else sees.
Sometimes through prayers that sound less like victory speeches and more like:
“Jesus, please help me make it through tonight.”
But there is something you are still fighting.
Something about your desires, body, loneliness, sexuality, marriage, singleness, history, or future that does not fit into an easy church testimony.
Do not run from Jesus because Christians have sometimes failed to represent Him well.
And do not remake Jesus simply because obedience hurts.
The Christ who is full of grace and truth.
Put all of it before Him and say:
“Jesus, I would rather belong to You than belong to the version of myself I am afraid to surrender.”
That prayer may cost you something.
But the One asking for your life is the One who first gave His life for you.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
The scandal may be what happened to you.
The scandal may be what you did.
The scandal may be what you desire.
The scandal may be the secret you buried.
The scandal may even be the cruelty of religious people who convinced you that Jesus wanted nothing to do with you.
But none of those things gets the final sentence.
At the cross, guilty people find forgiveness.
In the resurrection, dead things discover that death is not the end.
In Christ, the person everybody else reduced to a category receives a new name:
Because the blood of Jesus mattered more.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
Because one day nobody will stand before Christ and boast about how convincingly normal they appeared.
We will stand before the King.
And what will matter is whether we knew Him.
Whether His grace became more precious than our excuses.
Whether repentance became more precious than hiding.
Whether Christ became more precious than the identity we constructed without Him.
If something in these words exposed a place you have been hiding, don't perform for anyone.
Someone silently reading may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in complicated places.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if this truth can help one frightened person stop running from Christ, sharing it becomes a simple way of using the platform God has placed in your hands to point somebody toward Him.
But generosity can be worship when it flows from love for Christ.
And there is more available to help you grow.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is convinced that the complicated truth about their body, desires, past, or future has made them unreachable.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter of your story you are afraid to let anybody read—and when you surrender the pen to Him, your worst chapter does not have to become your final one.
